2027-06-15.title: Fifth Tuesday of the Apostles

readings: Blessed is anyone who takes no offense at me
2027-06-15.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven.
2027-06-15.verse: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor have good news brought to them.
theo: Today's Gospel opens with a sentence that fits this Season of the Apostles: “Now when Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples, he went on from there to teach and proclaim his message in their cities.” Matthew has just given us the great missionary discourse of chapter 10, in which Jesus sends the Twelve to proclaim the kingdom. The one who sends is himself the first missionary. Then the scene shifts to a prison. John the Baptist, who had prepared the way, is in Herod's fortress; the Jewish historian Josephus names it as Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea. From his cell John hears “what the Messiah was doing,” and he sends his disciples with a question: “Are you the one who is to come, or are we to wait for another?” It is a startling question from the man who had pointed to Jesus at the Jordan. John had announced an axe at the root of the trees and a fire that would burn the chaff (Matthew 3:10–12). Now he hears of a Messiah who heals, forgives and eats with sinners, while the prophet himself sits in chains. Some of the Fathers thought John asked for the sake of his disciples, so that they might go to Jesus themselves; others saw in the question the real night of a faithful man. Either way, the question is ours too, whenever God does not act as we expected.

Jesus does not answer with a title. He answers with what is happening: “Go and tell John what you hear and see: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor have good news brought to them.” Every phrase echoes the prophet Isaiah, who had promised that in the day of salvation “the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped” (Isaiah 35:5), and that the Anointed One would “bring good news to the oppressed” (Isaiah 61:1). John knew these Scriptures well; he would understand. The list ends not with the most spectacular sign, the raising of the dead, but with the poor hearing good news. That is the sign by which the kingdom can always be recognised, in every age and in every parish. Then comes a beatitude that is also a warning: “And blessed is anyone who takes no offense at me.” The word means to stumble over something in the road. Many stumble over Jesus: over his mercy to sinners, his silence before power, his Cross, and later over the weakness of his Church. Blessed is the one who keeps walking.

Paul's letter to the Colossians deals with a different stumbling block. Some teachers in Colossae were offering a religion of rules about food and festivals, of fear of “the elemental spirits of the universe,” and of special visions. Paul says: “If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the universe, why do you live as if you still belonged to the world? Why do you submit to regulations, ‘Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch’?” Such rules “refer to things that perish with use; they are simply human commands and teachings.” They have “an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-imposed piety, humility, and severe treatment of the body, but they are of no value in checking self-indulgence.” Paul is not condemning fasting or discipline. The Church has always fasted, as our Syro-Malankara brothers and sisters begin to do tomorrow in the Apostles' Fast, and as our own Church does in the Great Fast and on Wednesdays and Fridays. What Paul rejects is discipline cut off from Christ: rules that make us proud, rituals kept out of fear of unseen powers, practices that look holy but leave the heart unchanged. A Christian who has died and risen with Christ in Baptism does not need to fear auspicious hours or the evil eye, nor to buy God's favour by human regulations. Fasting in Christ is love that trains the heart; fasting without Christ is only hunger. John's question and Paul's warning meet here: the centre of our faith is not a system of rules or a Messiah of our own design, but the person of Jesus, seen in his works of mercy and followed without stumbling.

live: When God seems silent this week, look for one place where the poor are hearing good news, and thank God for it; better still, become that place for someone.
Choose one small fast this week, from food, screens or complaints, and offer it consciously in union with Christ, not out of fear or for show.
fathers: John was not ignorant of who Jesus was; but his disciples were jealous for their master and suspicious of Jesus. So John, about to die, sent them to Jesus, so that seeing his works with their own eyes they might believe and follow him. Like a good teacher, he handed his disciples on to Christ.

Many admired Christ's miracles but stumbled at his death. When they saw him humbled, mocked and crucified, they lost faith. Therefore he says, blessed is the one who is not scandalised in me: blessed is the one who, seeing my lowliness, still believes in my glory.
magis: Jesus accompanied his words with mighty works, wonders and signs, which show that the kingdom is present in him and attest that he is the promised Messiah; by his signs he did not come to abolish all evils here below, but to deliver us from the greatest slavery, sin.

Superstition is the deviation of religious feeling and of the practices it imposes; it can even affect true worship, as when one attributes an importance in some way magical to certain practices, otherwise lawful, apart from the interior dispositions they demand.

The way of perfection passes by way of the Cross; there is no holiness without renunciation and spiritual battle; spiritual progress entails the ascesis and mortification that gradually lead to living in the peace and joy of the Beatitudes.
saints: No saint's memorial is kept in the Syro-Malabar or the Latin calendar today. The Syro-Malankara calendar recalls the founding of the first church dedicated to the Holy Mother of God; tomorrow that Church begins the Apostles' Fast.

13–18 June: the fifth week of the Season of the Apostles. Sun 13: Fifth Sunday of the Apostles (in the Latin calendar the memorial of St Antony of Padua gives way to the Sunday). Wed 16: in the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church the Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu) begins. Sat 19: Sts Gervasius and Protasius are listed in the calendar. Sun 20: Sixth Sunday of the Apostles. Ahead: Thu 24 June, the Birth of John the Baptist; Tue 29 June, Sts Peter and Paul, a day of obligation.
2027-06-15.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you sent your apostles to proclaim the kingdom and you went ahead of them to teach and to heal. When we sit in the prisons of doubt and disappointment, as John did, send us your answer: open our eyes to see the blind receiving sight and the poor hearing good news. Keep us from stumbling over your humility and your Cross. You have made us die and rise with you in Baptism: take away every fear of unseen powers and every pride in our own practices, and let our fasting and prayer flow from love of you. Blessed are we if we take no offense at you. To the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Lord answers John's question again: here the One who is to come is present, humble under the signs of bread and wine. Blessed are those who do not stumble at his lowliness, but kneel and receive him.
This is the true discipline of the Christian: not human regulations, but communion with Christ who died and rose, and who changes the heart from within.

2027-06-15.question: Over what in Jesus or in his Church am I stumbling?

family.explain: John the Baptist was in prison. He sent his friends to ask Jesus, “Are you really the one God promised?” Jesus did not just say yes. He said, “Tell John what you see: blind people can see, lame people can walk, sick people are healed, and poor people hear the good news.” When we see people being helped and loved in Jesus' name, we can see that Jesus is really here.
family.intention: We pray for people in prison, and for all who find it hard to believe.
family.ask: Ask: “Where have we seen Jesus helping people this week?”

illus: A father from a parish near Pala prayed for two years for his little daughter, who had leukaemia. She died at the age of nine. For months he did not come to church. ‘If he is the Lord,’ he said to his brother, ‘why did he not do anything?’ One day the vicar, who knew he had a jeep, asked him to drive the parish palliative care nurses on their home visits, just for one week. He agreed, mostly to help the nurses. He saw a bedridden man in a tin-roofed house weep when the nurses washed him; an old woman alone who had not been visited by anyone for a month hold the volunteer's hand and pray; a family who could not afford medicines receive them. At the end of the week he told the vicar, ‘I still do not understand why my daughter died. But I have seen where he is.’ He has driven for the palliative team every Thursday since.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you are the one who is to come; we need not wait for another. Open our eyes to the signs of your kingdom, and keep us from stumbling. Holy Spirit, fill us as we pray. Amen.
share: When John heard in prison what the Messiah was doing (Matthew 11:2). In what prison of doubt or sorrow do I sit?
Go and tell John what you hear and see (Matthew 11:4). What have I seen the Lord doing in my life or my parish?
Blessed is anyone who takes no offense at me (Matthew 11:6). What about Jesus or his Church makes me stumble?
Why do you submit to regulations? (Colossians 2:20). Is my religion centred on Christ or on rules and fears?
pm.resp: Lord, we believe; help our unbelief.
interc: For the Church in this Season of the Apostles, that the poor may hear the good news through her.
For prisoners, and for all who are in the darkness of doubt, that the Lord may send them his answer.
For the blind, the disabled, the lepers and the sick, and for all who serve them.
For those bound by fear of evil spirits, bad omens or curses, that they may find peace in Christ.
For our Syro-Malankara brothers and sisters as they begin the Apostles' Fast tomorrow.
pm.close: Father, you sent your Son to bring good news to the poor and to heal the broken. Keep us from stumbling over his humility, make our devotion flow from union with him, and let us see and proclaim the signs of his kingdom. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, John the Baptist was in prison. He had prepared the way for Jesus, and now he sent a question: “Are you the one who is to come, or are we to wait for another?” (Matthew 11:3). Even a great prophet can have a dark night. If you have ever asked God, are you really there?, you are not alone.

Jesus did not scold John. He sent him an answer from the Scriptures: “the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor have good news brought to them” (Matthew 11:5). Look at what God is doing, he says. These are the signs of the kingdom.

Then Jesus adds: “blessed is anyone who takes no offense at me.” Many people stumble over Jesus: he is too humble, too merciful, he goes to the Cross. Blessed are we if we keep following him even when he does not act as we expected.

Saint Paul warns the Colossians against a religion of rules without Christ: do not touch, do not taste, do not handle. These rules look wise, but they do not change the heart. Fasting and discipline are good, but only when they come from love of Christ, not from pride or from fear of unseen powers. We have died and risen with Christ; we belong to him.

So let us keep our eyes on Jesus himself. Let us look for the signs of his kingdom, especially where the poor are loved, and let us become such signs for others. Blessed are we if we do not stumble over him. Amen.
kids: Children, John the Baptist was in prison and he was sad. He asked Jesus, “Are you really the one?” Jesus said, “Look: blind people see, sick people are healed, poor people hear good news!” When you help someone in Jesus' name, people can see that Jesus is real. Be a sign of Jesus this week!
